w: Fifteen subtropical hectares that predate the rest of the city's institutions - this is Durban's oldest public body and, by most reckonings, the oldest surviving botanical garden anywhere in Africa. Palms, cycads and orchid houses have quietly outlived everything built up around them since.
s: Africa's oldest botanical garden, still growing
_facts: Covers 15 hectares (37 acres) in a subtropical climate

w: Durban's civic anchor pulls triple duty - city hall, performing-arts venue and museum host, all under one historic roof in the heart of town. Council business, concerts and exhibitions have shared the same grand address for well over a century, one building doing three jobs at once.
s: One roof: town hall, theatre and museum
_facts: Historic city hall in Durban, KwaZulu-Natal
Listed types include performing arts center and museum building alongside city hall

w: White below, red above, and still working: this 21-metre concrete tower has stood unmanned on Umhlanga's beach since 1954, its main beam visible 24 nautical miles out to sea. A second, fixed red light does the safety job - if a ship's captain can see it, they are already too close to shore.
s: A lighthouse that still warns ships off Durban
_facts: 21 m tall, focal plane 25 m above high water; white below, red above
600,000 candela light visible 24 nautical miles, plus a fixed red light warning ships they are too close to Durban Harbour

w: Soofie Saheb arrived from India in 1895 and went on to found eleven mosques, thirteen madresas and a string of cemeteries across the country. He built this octagonal mausoleum for his own spiritual master, then was laid to rest inside it himself in 1911 - now ranked among South Africa's two holiest Muslim shrines.
s: Resting place of Soofie Saheb, a holiest shrine
_facts: Built by Soofie Saheb, who immigrated to South Africa in 1895
Soofie Saheb built 11 other mosques and 13 madresas and laid out numerous cemeteries
He died 29 June 1911 and is interred in the octagonal mausoleum, originally built for his spiritual master
Regarded as among the two holiest Muslim shrines in South Africa; mausoleum declared a National Monument 17 October 1980

w: Raised in 1842 by Captain Thomas Charlton Smith's troops, this fort was less about defence than message-sending - a visible British foothold meant to discourage Boer trekkers from planting a republic in Natal. An arsenal and barracks followed in 1858, garrisoned right through to the century's end.
s: An 1842 fort built to warn off the Boers
_facts: Built 1842 by Captain Thomas Charlton Smith's troops
Part of a British Empire visibility campaign to prevent Boers establishing a republic in Natal
Equipped with an arsenal and barracks in 1858; troops stationed there until end of the 19th century

w: Laid down stone by stone from 1902 to its 1904 dedication, this cathedral replaced a St Joseph's church that had served Durban's Catholics since 1881 and became the seat of the Archdiocese of Durban in 1951. Its neighbours tell their own story - a mosque next door, a market across the road.
s: A cathedral wedged between mosque and market
_facts: Catholic cathedral at 48 Cathedral Road, Durban; seat of the Metropolitan Archdiocese of Durban, created 1951 by the bull Suprema Nobis of Pope Pius XII
Built to replace an older St Joseph's church in use since 1881; first stone laid January 1902 by Bishop Charles Jolivet, dedicated November 1904
Adjacent to the Juma Masjid Mosque, with Victoria Street Market across the road
